title: LRU Cache
cue: Fixed-capacity key-value cache that evicts the least recently used key; get and put in O(1).
note: An instance of #144's hash map + ordering structure, where the ordering is a doubly linked list: the map points at nodes, so get moves a node to the front and put evicts from the tail in O(1). The pointer surgery (unlink, push front, update an existing key) is where bugs live; #422's sentinel nodes remove most of the edge cases.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
cue: Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (not contiguous).
note: Unlike #73, the best run ending at i can extend from any earlier j, not just i−1, so the plain DP is O(n²). The O(n log n) version keeps tails[k] = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1 and updates it with #139's lower_bound; tails is not itself an LIS, which is the part people get wrong.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
cue: Cheapest route from src to dst using at most k intermediate stops.
note: Plain Dijkstra with a visited set is wrong: a costlier path with fewer stops may be the only one within the limit. Run k+1 rounds of Bellman-Ford relaxing from a copy of the previous round, or BFS by layers like #156 over (node, stops) states. Unlike #200's bottleneck path, the constraint is on edge count, not edge weight.

title: Edit Distance
cue: Minimum insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another.
note: The canonical #416 two-sequence DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes, a match carries the diagonal and a mismatch takes 1 + min of the three neighbours. The hard part is mapping each operation to the right neighbour and initialising row/column 0 as pure inserts/deletes.

title: Word Break
cue: Can a string be split into a sequence of dictionary words?
note: 1-D DP like #323, but dp[i] (prefix of length i is breakable) looks back to every j with dp[j] true and s[j:i] in the dictionary, not just i−1 and i−2. Bound j by the longest word, or walk a #284 trie forward from each true position. Greedy longest-match fails.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
cue: Length of the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, in O(n).
note: Set membership like #461, plus the key insight: only start counting from x when x−1 is not in the set, so each run is walked once and the nested loop is still O(n) total. Sorting gives O(n log n) and is the trap answer.

title: Construct Binary Tree From Preorder And Inorder Traversal
cue: Rebuild a binary tree from its preorder and inorder sequences (unique values).
note: Same family as #305, but it takes two sequences: preorder's next element is the root, and its position in inorder splits the left and right subtrees. A value→index map plus a moving preorder pointer makes it O(n); slicing arrays makes it O(n²), and the off-by-one in the split is where it usually breaks.

title: Interleaving String
cue: Can s3 be formed by interleaving s1 and s2 while keeping each one's order?
note: Two-sequence DP like #416, but the third string is indexed implicitly: dp[i][j] means s1[:i] and s2[:j] form s3[:i+j]. It is effectively #272's grid path where each right/down step must match the next char of s3. Check the lengths first; greedy two-pointer matching fails on ties.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
cue: Can the array be split into two subsets with equal sums?
note: The reformulation is the insight: it is #95's subset sum with target total/2 (odd total means false). Use a 1-D boolean dp iterated backwards over sums so each number is used once, or a bitset shift.

title: Target Sum
cue: Number of ways to put + or − before each number so the total equals target.
note: Brute force is #85-style 2^n choices. Reformulate: if P is the plus set, sum(P) = (total + target)/2, so it becomes #95 subset counting. Guard against odd parity and |target| > total; zeros double the count, which the dp handles but ad-hoc memo shortcuts often miss.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
cue: Largest product of a contiguous subarray (negatives and zeros allowed).
note: Kadane like #73, but a negative can flip the smallest product into the largest, so track both the max and min product ending at i (swap them on a negative). Zeros reset both.

title: Decode Ways
cue: Count ways to decode a digit string where 1–26 map to A–Z.
note: Same recurrence shape as #323's 1-D counting (take one digit or two), but the edge cases are the problem: '0' cannot stand alone, '06' is not valid, and only 10–26 count as two-digit codes. A leading '0' or '00' makes the answer 0.

title: Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock With Cooldown
cue: Max profit with unlimited trades but a one-day cooldown after each sale.
note: #414's one-pass greedy breaks because the cooldown couples days. Model it as a state machine (holding, just sold, resting) with per-day transitions, like #459's take/skip with three states. Reading yesterday's values rather than today's partially updated ones is the usual bug.

title: Coin Change II
cue: Number of coin combinations (order doesn't matter) that sum to an amount.
note: Unbounded #95 knapsack counting. The trap is loop order: coins in the outer loop counts combinations; amount in the outer loop counts permutations (that is Combination Sum IV, closer to #323).

title: Gas Station
cue: Find the start index from which you can drive once around a circular route of gas stations.
note: Two insights: a solution exists iff total gas ≥ total cost, and if the running tank goes negative at i, no start between the current start and i works, so jump the start to i+1. A one-pass prefix-sum argument, close in spirit to #73's reset-on-negative.

title: Valid Parenthesis String
cue: Is a string of '(', ')' and '*' balanced, where '*' can be '(', ')' or empty?
note: #249's single counter breaks because '*' is three-way. Track the range [lo, hi] of possible open counts: '(' raises both, ')' lowers both, '*' lowers lo and raises hi; fail if hi < 0, clamp lo at 0, and require lo == 0 at the end. Two-stack and O(n²) DP versions also work.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
cue: Cells from which water can flow downhill to both the top/left ocean and the bottom/right ocean.
note: Searching from every cell is O((mn)²). Reverse the flow: a #131-style multi-source search from each ocean's border, moving uphill (to neighbours ≥ current), then intersect the two reachable sets.

title: Task Scheduler
cue: Minimum time slots to run tasks when identical tasks need n idle slots between them.
note: Starts from #356's frequency count, but the answer is a counting argument: (maxFreq − 1) × (n + 1) + (number of tasks with maxFreq), floored at the task count. A max-heap plus cooldown-queue simulation also works, but the formula is the insight interviewers probe.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
cue: Longest substring that can become all one letter after at most k replacements.
note: A longest-window problem like #11, but validity is window length − count of the most frequent char ≤ k. The subtle part: maxFreq never needs to decrease when shrinking, because only a larger maxFreq can produce a longer answer.

title: Car Fleet
cue: How many groups of cars reach the destination, given cars can't pass and merge when they catch up.
note: Reformulate as arrival times: sort by position descending (#477-style), compute (target − pos)/speed, and a car starts a new fleet only if its time is strictly greater than the fleet ahead. That is a monotonic stack of times like #13, though a single running max suffices.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
cue: Minimum total Manhattan distance to connect all points into one network.
note: A minimum spanning tree on a complete graph. Kruskal reuses #18's idea (process edges in order, union until connected) but materialises O(n²) edges; Prim's with a heap or an O(n²) array scan suits the dense graph better. Unlike #109, which edges you pick matters, not just which points end up together.

title: Find The Duplicate Number
cue: Find the one repeated value among n+1 numbers in 1..n without modifying the array and in O(1) space.
note: The reformulation: treat i → nums[i] as a linked list; the duplicate is the entrance to its cycle, found with Floyd's tortoise-and-hare plus a second pass from the start. An O(n log n) alternative is #92's binary search on the answer (count values ≤ mid). #325's XOR trick fails because the duplicate can appear more than twice.

title: Search In Rotated Sorted Array
cue: Find a target in a sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot, in O(log n).
note: #349-style: at each step one half is sorted; if the target lies in that half's range go there, else go to the other half. The <= vs < comparisons when lo == mid are the classic bug; Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array is the warm-up variant.

title: Copy List With Random Pointer
cue: Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes also have a random pointer to any node or null.
note: Random pointers can point forward, so copies can't be wired in one pass. Map old→new in a hash map over two passes, or use the O(1)-space trick: interleave each copy after its original, set copy.random = orig.random.next, then unweave. More pointer juggling than #506's reversal.

title: Design Twitter
cue: Mini Twitter: post, follow/unfollow, and fetch the 10 most recent tweets from yourself and followees.
note: The feed is #514's merging-sequences-behind-an-API: each followee's tweets are a time-sorted list, and the top 10 come from a k-way heap merge like #5. Details: a global timestamp, implicitly following yourself, and unfollowing yourself being a no-op.

title: Jump Game II
cue: Minimum number of jumps to reach the last index when nums[i] is the max jump length from i.
note: It is #156's BFS by layers without a queue: the current layer is the index range reachable in j jumps, and the next layer extends to the farthest i + nums[i] within it. Seeing the implicit BFS is the insight; the O(n²) DP is the trap answer.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
cue: Longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.
note: #508 interval DP (dp[i][j] = ends match and dp[i+1][j−1]) works in O(n²) space, but expand-around-center is simpler: 2n−1 centres covering odd and even lengths. Forgetting even-length centres is the usual bug; Palindromic Substrings is the same expansion, counting instead of maxing.

title: 3Sum
cue: All unique triplets that sum to zero.
note: #420's k-sum family: sort, fix i, then inward pointers for the pair. What trips people is deduplication without a set of tuples: skip equal nums[i], and after a hit skip equal values on both pointers.

title: Reorder List
cue: Reorder L0→L1→…→Ln into L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1→… in place.
note: Combines three steps: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half (#506), then merge the halves alternately. Cutting the first half's tail is the step people forget, which leaves a cycle.

title: Product of Array Except Self
cue: For each index, the product of all other elements, without division and in O(n).
note: Like #468's precomputation, but with products and excluding i: answer[i] = prefix product before i × suffix product after i. In O(1) extra space, write prefixes into the output, then multiply in a running suffix from the right; division fails on zeros.

title: Container With Most Water
cue: Two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water.
note: Inward pointers like #420, but the array isn't sorted and the move rule needs a proof: always move the shorter line, since any container that keeps it is narrower and can't be taller. Trapping Rain Water builds on the same idea.

title: Combination Sum II
cue: All unique combinations summing to target, each number used at most once, input has duplicates.
note: #85's pick-from-a-candidate-list plus duplicate handling: sort, and at each recursion level skip a candidate equal to the previous one at that level (i > start and nums[i] == nums[i−1]). The same trick drives Subsets II.

title: Detect Squares
cue: Stream of points; count axis-aligned squares a query point forms with stored points (duplicates count).
note: Keep a counter of points. For a query, treat each stored point as the diagonal corner (|dx| == |dy| ≠ 0) and multiply the counts of the two remaining corners: a #515-style partner lookup generalised to 2D. Multiplicity from duplicate points is the fiddly part.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
cue: Is a binary tree a valid BST (whole left subtree < node < whole right subtree)?
note: Comparing a node only with its children is the trap. Either pass (low, high) bounds down like #389's accumulators, or use #413's in-order traversal and check it is strictly increasing. Use None or infinite bounds, not INT_MIN/INT_MAX, since node values can equal them.

title: Surrounded Regions
cue: Capture 'O' regions fully enclosed by 'X'; regions touching the border survive.
note: Flood fill like #17, but reversed: start from border 'O's (#131-style multi-source) and mark the survivors, then flip every unmarked 'O'. Deciding enclosure region by region is messier.

title: Hand of Straights
cue: Can the cards be split into groups of groupSize consecutive values?
note: Partner lookup in a counter like #515, extended to a run of groupSize: the smallest remaining card must start a group, so repeatedly take the min (sorted keys or a heap) and decrement the next groupSize−1 values. Seeing that the smallest card's role is forced is the insight.

title: Partition Labels
cue: Split a string into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in only one part.
note: Each letter defines an interval [first, last], and the parts are #202's merged intervals. In one pass: record each letter's last index, extend the current end to max(last[c]), and cut when i == end.

title: House Robber II
cue: Max sum of non-adjacent houses arranged in a circle (first and last are adjacent).
note: #459's take/skip with a circular twist: the first and last can't both be taken, so run the linear solution on nums[1:] and nums[:-1] and take the max. Handle n == 1 separately.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
cue: If a cell is 0, zero its entire row and column, in place.
note: Easy with O(m+n) extra sets; the O(1)-space version stores markers in the first row and column and needs a separate flag for whether row 0 or column 0 itself had a zero. Order matters: zero the inner cells first, then the first row and column.

title: Spiral Matrix
cue: Return a matrix's elements in clockwise spiral order.
note: No algorithmic insight, just fiddly bounds: shrink top/bottom/left/right after each side, and re-check top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right before walking the bottom row and left column, or single rows and columns get duplicated.

title: Rotate Image
cue: Rotate an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place.
note: The reformulation: clockwise rotation = transpose, then reverse each row (#472's in-place reverse). The direct four-way cycle swap, layer by layer, also works but its index arithmetic is error-prone.

title: Sum of Two Integers
cue: Add two integers without using + or −.
note: a ^ b is the sum without carries and (a & b) << 1 is the carry; loop until the carry is zero: #173's column arithmetic done in binary, all bits at once. In Python you must mask to 32 bits and convert back for negatives, which is the real difficulty.
